summary: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection normally needs a control session between two systems. This RFC lets a system use the BFD Echo function on its own, with no matching control session at the other end. It helps quickly detect forwarding path failures where setting up full BFD on both sides is not practical.

plainLanguage.summary: You throw a ball at a wall and catch it when it bounces back. If it does not come back, something is blocking the way. Nobody needs to stand behind the wall.

subtitle: Use BFD Echo on its own: one side runs BFD and the other just loops packets back.

tldr.problem: BFD normally needs both ends of a link to run the protocol, but some devices, such as servers running virtual machines or IoT devices, cannot support full BFD.
tldr.mechanism: The local device sends BFD Control packets to the BFD Echo port with its own IP address as destination, and the neighbor loops them back through ordinary IP forwarding. The local device runs the BFD state machine on the looped packets.
tldr.outcome: A device can quickly detect loss of connectivity to a one-hop neighbor that has no BFD support, but only over a single IP hop. The RFC updates RFC 5880.

today: RFC 9747 is a Proposed Standard from March 2025 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 5880 and no later RFC is listed as updating it.

sections.title: Affiliated and Unaffiliated Echo
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) detects faults on the path between adjacent forwarding engines. It has Asynchronous and Demand modes, plus an optional Echo function where the remote system loops the sender's packets back. If several consecutive Echo packets do not return, the session is declared Down.

The RFC names two ways to use Echo. Affiliated BFD Echo needs full BFD on both devices and is unchanged. Unaffiliated BFD Echo needs only the local device to support BFD. It sends BFD Control packets over the Echo port, using Asynchronous mode procedures with modifications, with one of its own IP addresses as the destination, so the neighbor returns them.

This method checks connectivity to a device over a specific interface. It does not verify that a specific IP address at that device is available. It works for a single IP hop over IPv4 and IPv6, because over multiple hops the first hop would loop the packets back.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally two players both need to know the game. Here only one player needs to know the game, and the other just bounces the ball back.

sections.title: How Unaffiliated Echo Works
sections.content:
Device A supports BFD. Device B is a regular IP forwarder. A sends Unaffiliated BFD Echo packets and B loops them back by normal IP forwarding, without intercepting them or parsing any BFD field. A can then rapidly detect a connectivity loss to B. No BFD state is coordinated between the two ends, so strictly this is not a BFD session, though A can treat it as one.

The session on A MUST follow the BFD state machine of RFC 5880 Section 6.2, except that the received state comes from looped-back packets A itself generated. The AdminDown state is not used. Packets use UDP destination port 3785 and the encapsulation of RFC 5881. Standard Asynchronous procedures apply, including validation and authentication.

Packets with a zeroed Your Discriminator are matched to a session by source IP address or UDP source port. Once the remote system loops back the local discriminator, matching uses Your Discriminator only. Packets MUST be sent with TTL or Hop Limit 255, and received packets MUST have 254 or be dropped.

A starts with slow transmission, no greater than one packet per second, until the session is Up, then uses the provisioned interval. If a Detect Mult number of packets fail to arrive while Up, A sets bfd.SessionState to Down and bfd.LocalDiag to 2 (Echo Function Failed). Going Down resumes slow transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: You send yourself a message through a friend who just passes it along unopened. If your messages stop coming back several times in a row, you know the road to your friend is broken.

sections.title: Packet Field Values
sections.content:
An Unaffiliated BFD Echo packet reuses the BFD Control packet format. Every field MUST be filled with a definite value, even if the receiver ignores it, so that uninitialized memory is not exposed.

  • My Discriminator: the provisioned local discriminator.
  • Your Discriminator: 0 at first, then the My Discriminator value looped back.
  • Desired Min TX Interval and Required Min RX Interval: a specific value, suggested 1 second (1,000,000 microseconds). They MUST be ignored on receipt and not used for Detection Time.
  • Required Min Echo RX Interval: a specific value, suggested 0, ignored on receipt.
  • Detect Mult: the provisioned maximum number of consecutively lost packets.

The transmit interval while Up MUST be provisioned on device A. How device B is set up to loop packets back is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every blank on the form must be filled in with something, even blanks nobody will read, so no old scribbles leak out.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 5880
sections.content:
Unaffiliated Echo reuses the Echo function without Asynchronous or Demand mode. Only the local system runs BFD, and the remote system treats Echo packets as ordinary data. To allow this, the RFC changes several passages of RFC 5880 with OLD TEXT and NEW TEXT blocks.

The changes are mostly clarifications. Section 3.2 now says the Echo function can run independently, with neither Asynchronous nor Demand mode. Sections 6.1, 6.4, 6.8, 6.8.3 and 6.8.9 now say that their existing Echo rules apply when a system is using Echo with Asynchronous or Demand mode. For instance, the rule that Echo packets MUST NOT be sent unless the remote system advertises a nonzero Required Min Echo RX Interval applies to those modes, not to Unaffiliated Echo.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook assumed both players always sat at the table. A few lines were reworded to say the bounce-back game can also be played alone.

sections.title: Operational Notes
sections.content:
All operational considerations from RFC 5880 apply. Because traffic is paced by configuration, there is no real possibility of congestion, and congesting the path would defeat the check anyway.

The device that loops packets back must perform IP forwarding. This is typical for routers but may not be on by default for hosts. An Unaffiliated Echo session can coexist with other BFD sessions on the local system, but its remote system must differ from the remote system of any other BFD session, and discriminators must differ across sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The friend who bounces your messages must be willing to pass them along. Many routers do this by default, but a plain computer may need to be told.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5880 and RFC 5881 apply. The remote device cannot use Unicast Strict Reverse Path Forwarding (RFC 3704), or the looped packets might fail the check.

Echo packets can be spoofed, and a DoS attacker could send spoofed Unaffiliated BFD Echo packets to the loopback device, so some form of authentication SHOULD be used. Since the packets are also BFD Control packets, including the Authentication Section is RECOMMENDED. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could throw fake balls at the wall. A secret stamp on your own balls lets you tell yours from fakes.
